Blow-up solutions and peakons to a generalized μ\mu-Camassa-Holm integrable equation

Changzheng Qu Address: Changzheng Qu
Department of Mathematics, Ningbo University, Ningbo 315211, P. R. China Email address: quchangzheng@nbu.edu.cn , Ying Fu Address: Ying Fu
Department of Mathematics
Northwest University
Xi’an 710069
P. R. China Email address: fuying@nwu.edu.cn and Yue Liu Address: Yue Liu
Department of Mathematics, University of Texas, Arlington, TX 76019-0408 Email address: yliu@uta.edu
Abstract.

Consideration here is a generalized μ\mu-type integrable equation, which can be regarded as a generalization to both the μ\mu-Camassa-Holm and modified μ\mu-Camassa-Holm equations. It is shown that the proposed equation is formally integrable with the Lax-pair and the bi-Hamiltonian structure and its scale limit is an integrable model of hydrodynamical systems describing short capillary-gravity waves. Local well-posedness of the Cauchy problem in the suitable Sobolev space is established by the viscosity method. Existence of peaked traveling-wave solutions and formation of singularities of solutions for the equation are investigated. It is found that the equation admits a single peaked soliton and multi-peakon solutions. The effects of varying μ\mu-Camassa-Holm and modified μ\mu-Camassa-Holm nonlocal nonlinearities on blow-up criteria and wave breaking are illustrated in detail. Our analysis relies on the method of characteristics and conserved quantities and is proceeded with a priori differential estimates.

Keywords: μ\mu-Camassa-Holm equation, modified μ\mu-Camassa-Holm equation, integrable system, blow-up, wave breaking, peakons.

AMS Subject Classification (2000): 35B30,35G25

1. Introduction

In this paper, we are concerned with the following new integrable partial differential equation

OPENmt+k1​(2​μ​(u)​u−ux2)​m)x+k2​(2​m​ux+u​mx)+γ​ux=0,m_{t}+k_{1}\big(2\mu(u)u-u^{2}_{x})m\big)_{x}+k_{2}(2mu_{x}+um_{x})+\gamma u_{x}=0, (1.1)

where u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is a function of time tt and a single spatial variable xx, and

m=μ⁡(u)−ux​x,μ⁡(u)=∫𝕊u⁡(t,x)​𝑑x,m=\mu(u)-u_{xx},\quad\mu(u)=\int_{{S}}u(t,x)dx, (1.2)

with 𝕊=ℝ/ℤ{{S}}={{R}}/{{Z}} which denotes the unit circle on ℝ2{{R}}^{2}. Eq.(1.1) is reduced to the μ\mu-Camassa-Holm (CH) equation [30]

mt+2​m​ux+u​mx+γ​ux=0,m_{t}+2mu_{x}+um_{x}+\gamma u_{x}=0, (1.3)

for k1=0k_{1}=0 and k2=1,k_{2}=1, and the modified μ\mu-CH equation [42]

mt+((2​μ​(u)​u−ux2)​m)x+γ​ux=0,m_{t}+\big((2\mu(u)u-u^{2}_{x})m\big)_{x}+\gamma u_{x}=0, (1.4)

for k2=0k_{2}=0 and k1=1k_{1}=1, respectively.

It is known that the CH equation [4, 25] of the following form

mt+u​mx+2​ux​m+γ​ux=0,withm=u−ux​xm_{t}+um_{x}+2u_{x}m+\gamma u_{x}=0,\quad\text{with}\quad m=u-u_{xx} (1.5)

was proposed as a model for the unidirectional propagation of the shallow water waves over a flat bottom (see also [15, 28]), with u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) representing the height of the water’s free surface in terms of non-dimensional variables. It is completely integrable with a bi-Hamiltonian structure and an infinite number of conservation laws [4, 25]. It is of interest to note that the CH equation can also be derived by tri-Hamiltonian duality from the KdV equation (a number of additional examples of dual integrable systems derived applying the method of tri-Hamiltonian duality can be found in [24, 39]). The CH equation has two remarkable features: existence of peakon and multi-peakons [1, 4, 5] (when γ=0\gamma=0) and breaking waves, i.e., wave profile remains bounded while its slope becomes unbounded in finite time [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 33]. Geometrically, the CH equation describes the geodesic flows on the Bott-Virasoro group for the case γ≠0\gamma\not=0 [37, 45] and on the diffeomorphism group of the unit circle under H1H^{1} metric for the case γ=0\gamma=0 [31], respectively. Note that the two geometric descriptions are not analogous: for γ=0\gamma=0 (on the diffeomorphism group) the Riemannian exponential map is a local chart, but this is not the case for γ≠0\gamma\neq 0 (on the Bott-Virasoro group) cf. the discussion in [14]. The CH equation also arises from a non-stretching invariant planar curve flow in the centro-equiaffine geometry [7, 38]. Well-posedness and wave breaking of the CH equation were studied extensively, and many interesting results have been obtained, see [9, 11, 12, 13, 33], for example. The μ\mu-CH equation (1.3) was first introduced by Khesin, Lenells and Misiolek [30]. They verified that the μ\mu-CH equation is bi-Hamiltonian and admits cusped and smooth traveling wave solutions. In [32], it was shown that the μ\mu-CH equation also admits single peakon and multi-peakons. Interestingly, the μ\mu-CH equation describes a geodesic flow on diffeomorphism group over 𝕊{{S}} with certain metric. Its well-posedness and blow up were investigated in [23, 30].

Another well-known integrable equation admitting peakons with quadratic nonlinearities is the Degasperis-Procesi (DP) equation [17], which takes the form

mt+u​mx+3​ux​m=0,m=u−ux​x.m_{t}+um_{x}+3u_{x}m=0,\;\;m=u-u_{xx}. (1.6)

It is regarded as a model for nonlinear shallow water dynamics, which can also be obtained from the governing equations for water waves [15]. Its asymptotic accuracy is the same as for the Camassa-Holm shallow water equation. More interestingly, it admits the shock peakons in both periodic [20] and non-periodic settings [35]. Wave breaking phenomena and global existence of solutions for the Degasperis-Procesi equation were investigated in [8, 18, 19, 20, 35, 36]. The μ\mu-version of the DP equation was introduced by Lenells, Misiolek and Tiğlay [32], which takes the form (1.6) with mm replaced by m=μ⁡(u)−ux​xm=\mu(u)-u_{xx}. Its integrability, well-posedness, blow up and existence of peakons were investigated in [23, 32].

It is noted that all nonlinear terms in the CH and DP equations are quadratic. So it is of great interest to find such integrable equations with cubic and higher-order nonlinear terms. The CH equation can be obtained by the tri-Hamiltonian duality approach from the bi-Hamiltonian structure of the KdV equation [39]. Similarly, the approach applied to the modified KdV equation then yields the so-called modified CH equation [39, 22, 40]

mt+((u2−ux2)​m)x=0,m=u−ux​x,m_{t}+\big((u^{2}-u^{2}_{x})m\big)_{x}=0,\quad m=u-u_{xx}, (1.7)

which has cubic nonlinearities, and is integrable with the Lax-pair and the bi-Hamiltonian structure. It was shown that the modified CH equation has a single peaked soliton and multi-peakons with a different character than those of the CH equation [27], and it also has new features of blow-up criterion and wave breaking mechanism. The μ\mu-version of the modified CH equation, called the modified μ\mu-CH equation

mt+((2​u​μ​(u)−ux2)​m)x=0,m=μ⁡(u)−ux​x,m_{t}+\big((2u\mu(u)-u^{2}_{x})m\big)_{x}=0,\quad m=\mu(u)-u_{xx}, (1.8)

was introduced in [42]. It is also formally integrable with the bi-Hamiltonian structure and the Lax-pair, and arises from a non-stretching planar curve flows in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} [42]. On the other hand, its local well-posedness, wave breaking, existence of peakons and their stability were discussed in [42, 34]. As an extension of both the CH and modified CH equations, an integrable equation with both quadratic and cubic nonlinearities has been introduced by Fokas [22], which takes the form

OPENmt+k1​((u2−ux2))​m)x+k2​(2​ux​m+u​mx)=0,m=u−ux​x.m_{t}+k_{1}\big((u^{2}-u_{x}^{2}))m\big)_{x}+k_{2}(2u_{x}m+um_{x})=0,\quad m=u-u_{xx}. (1.9)

It was shown by Qiao et al [41] that Eq.(1.9) is integrable with the Lax-pair and the bi-Hamiltonian structure. Its peaked solitons were also obtained in [41]. Indeed, Eq.(1.9) can be obtained by the tri-Hamiltonian duality approach from the bi-Hamiltonian structure of the Gardner equation

mt+k1​u2​ux+k2​u​ux=0.m_{t}+k_{1}u^{2}u_{x}+k_{2}uu_{x}=0. (1.10)

It was noticed in [27] and [42] that the short-pulse equation as an approximation of the Maxwell equation [44],

vx​t+12​(v2​vx)x+v=0v_{xt}+\frac{1}{2}(v^{2}v_{x})_{x}+v=0 (1.11)

is a scale limit of both the modified CH equation (1.7) and the modified μ\mu-CH (1.8) equation.

The goal of the present paper is to investigate whether or not the generalized μ\mu-version (1.1) with two different nonlocal nonlinearities has similar remarkable properties as the CH equation (1.5) and the modified CH equation (1.7) as well as their μ\mu-versions. As is well known, in order for persistent structures and properties to exist in such equations, there must be a delicate nonlinear/nonlocal balance, even in the absence of linear dispersion with γ=0.\gamma=0. Indeed, it is shown in Theorem 4.1 that Eq.(1.1) admits a single peaked soliton and multi-peakon solutions even the parameters k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} have a different sign.

On the other hand, it is found that those two parameters k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} corresponding to the modified μ\mu-CH cubic and μ\mu-CH quadratic nonlinearities respectively play an important role in the effects of varying nonlocal nonlinearites on the finite blow-up of solutions, or wave breaking. It is well known that wave breaking relies crucially on strong nonlinear and nonlocal dispersion. Indeed, in the case of the CH equation with the quadratic nonlinearity, the wave cannot break in finite time when the momentum potential m=(1−∂x2)um=(1-\partial_{x}^{2})u keeps positive initially [9]. The breaking wave, however, occurs for the modified CH equation with the cubic nonlinearity, even mm is positive initially [27]. Those of key different features of wave breaking make our investigation on the wave breaking to the generalized μ\mu-version (1.1) more interesting but the analysis more challenging.

In view of the transport theory, the key issue to obtain the wave breaking result (Theorem 7.2) is to derive a priori differential estimate so that the slope k1​ux​m+k2​uxk_{1}u_{x}m+k_{2}u_{x} is unbounded below. Rather, the nonlocal nature and mixed strong nonlinearites of the problem prohibit the use of classical blow-up approaches. To this end, we shall adopt the method of characteristics with conservative quantities and the new mechanism of a priori differential inequalities to control higher nonlocal nonlinearities. This new approach is expected to have more applications to deal with wave breaking of the other nonlinear dispersive model wave equations with higher nonlocal nonlinearities.

The outline of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, integrability of Eq.(1.1) is illuminated. Section 3 is devoted to some basic facts and results, which will be used in the subsequent sections. In Section 4, existence of the single peakon and multi-peakons of Eq.(1.1) are demonstrated. Local well-posedness in the Sobolev space to the Cauchy problem associated with Eq.(1.1) is then obtained in Section 5. Blow-up criterion for strong solutions is established in Section 6. Finally in Section 7, with a new blow-up mechanism, sufficient conditions for wave breaking of strong solutions in finite time are described in detail.

2. Integrability and conservation laws

In this section, we study integrability of Eq.(1.1). On one hand, Eq.(1.1) admits a bi-Hamiltonian structure, and it is formally integrable. Indeed, it can be written in the bi-Hamiltonian form

mt=J​δ​H1δ​m=K​δ​H2δ​m,m_{t}=J\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta m}=K\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta m},

where

J=−k1∂xm∂x−1m∂x−k2(m∂x+∂xm)−12γ∂x,andK=−∂A=∂x3,J=-k_{1}\,\partial_{x}\,m\,\partial_{x}^{-1}\,m\,\partial_{x}-k_{2}(m\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}m)-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\partial_{x},\qquad{\rm and}\qquad K=-\partial A=\partial_{x}^{3},

are compatible Hamiltonian operators, while

H1=12​∫𝕊m​u​dx,andH2=∫𝕊(μ2​(u)​u2+μ⁡(u)​u​ux2−112​ux4)​𝑑x+k2​∫𝕊(μ⁡(u)​u+12​u​ux2)​𝑑x\begin{array}[]{c}H_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{{{S}}}mu\,dx,\qquad\text{and}\\[8.5359pt] H_{2}=\int_{{{S}}}\left(\mu^{2}(u)u^{2}+\mu(u)uu^{2}_{x}-\frac{1}{12}u^{4}_{x}\right)\,dx+k_{2}\int_{{{S}}}(\mu(u)u+\frac{1}{2}uu_{x}^{2})dx\end{array} (2.1)

are the corresponding Hamiltonian functionals. According to Magri’s theorem [38], the associated recursion operator ℛ=J⋅K−1{\mathcal{R}}=J\cdot K^{-1} produces a hierarchy of commuting Hamiltonian functionals and bi-Hamiltonian flows.

On the other hand, Eq.(1.1) admits the following Lax-pair

(ψ1ψ2)x=U⁡(m)​(ψ1ψ2),(ψ1ψ2)t=V⁡(m,u,λ)​(ψ1ψ2),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{1}\\ \psi_{2}\end{pmatrix}_{x}=U(m)\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{1}\\ \psi_{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\quad\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{1}\\ \psi_{2}\end{pmatrix}_{t}=V(m,u,\lambda)\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{1}\\ \psi_{2}\end{pmatrix},

where UU and VV are given by

U⁡(m,λ)=(0λ​m−k1​λ​m−k2​λ0),\displaystyle U(m,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda\,m\\[5.69046pt] -k_{1}\lambda\,m-k_{2}\lambda&0\end{pmatrix},

and

V⁡(m,u,λ)=(−12​ux−μ⁡(u)2​λ−k1​λ​(2​μ​(u)​u−ux2)​m−k2​λ​u​mG12​k2​ux),\displaystyle V(m,u,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}u_{x}&-\frac{\mu(u)}{2\lambda}-k_{1}\lambda(2\mu(u)u-u^{2}_{x})m-k_{2}\lambda um\\[5.69046pt] G&\frac{1}{2}k_{2}u_{x}\end{pmatrix},

for γ=0\gamma=0 with

G=k2​(12​λ+λ​k2​u)+12​λ​k1​μ​(u)+k12​λ​(2​u​μ​(u)−ux2)​m+k1​k2​λ​(2​u​μ​(u)−ux2−u​m),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} G=&\;k_{2}\big(\frac{1}{2\lambda}+\lambda k_{2}u\big)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}k_{1}\mu(u)+k_{1}^{2}\lambda(2u\mu(u)-u_{x}^{2})m\\ &+k_{1}k_{2}\lambda\big(2u\mu(u)-u_{x}^{2}-um\big),\end{aligned}

and

U⁡(m,λ)=(−−12​γ​λλ​m−k1​λ​m−k2​λ−12​γ​λ),\displaystyle U(m,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}-\sqrt{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma}\lambda&\lambda\,m\\ -k_{1}\lambda\,m-k_{2}\lambda&\sqrt{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma}\lambda\end{pmatrix},

and

V⁡(m,u,λ)=(ABG−A),\displaystyle V(m,u,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ G&-A\end{pmatrix},

for γ≠0\gamma\not=0 with

A=14​−2​γ​(λ−1+2​λ​k1​(2​u​μ​(u)−ux2)+2​λ​k2​u)−12​k2​ux,\displaystyle A=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{-2\gamma}\big(\lambda^{-1}+2\lambda k_{1}(2u\mu(u)-u_{x}^{2})+2\lambda k_{2}u\big)-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}u_{x},
B=−μ2​λ+12​−2​γ​ux−k1​λ​(2​u​μ​(u)−ux2)​m−λ​k2​u​m.\displaystyle B=-\frac{\mu}{2\lambda}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{-2\gamma}u_{x}-k_{1}\lambda(2u\mu(u)-u_{x}^{2})m-\lambda k_{2}um.

Let us now consider a scale limit of Eq.(1.1). Applying the scaling transformation

x⟼ϵ​x,\displaystyle x\longmapsto\epsilon\,x,   t⟼ϵ−1​t,\displaystyle t\longmapsto\epsilon^{-1}t,   u⟼ϵ2​u\displaystyle u\longmapsto\epsilon^{2}u

u⁡(t,x)=u0​(t,x)+ϵ​u1​(t,x)+ϵ2​u2​(t,x)+⋯u(t,x)=u_{0}(t,x)+\epsilon\,u_{1}(t,x)+\epsilon^{2}\,u_{2}(t,x)+\>\cdots

in powers of the small parameter ϵ\epsilon, the leading order term u0​(t,x)u_{0}(t,x) satisfies

−u0,x​x​t+k1​(u0,x2​u0,x​x)x−k2​(u0,x​u0,x​x+u0​u0,x​x​x)+γ​u0,x=0.-u_{0,xxt}+k_{1}(u_{0,x}^{2}u_{0,xx})_{x}-k_{2}\big(u_{0,x}u_{0,xx}+u_{0}u_{0,xxx}\big)+\gamma u_{0,x}=0.

It follows that v=u0,xv=u_{0,x} satisfies the following integrable equation

vx​t−k1​vx2​vx​x+k2​(v​vx​x+12​vx2)−γ​v=0,v_{xt}-k_{1}v_{x}^{2}v_{xx}+k_{2}(vv_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}v_{x}^{2})-\gamma v=0,

which describes asymptotic dynamics of a short capillary-gravity wave [21], where v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) denotes the fluid velocity on the surface.

In this section, we are concerned with the following Cauchy problem of Eq.(1.1) with γ=0\gamma=0

{mt+k1(2μ(u)u−u2x)m)x+k2(2mux+umx)=0,t>0,x∈ℝ,u(0,x)=u0(x),m=μ(u)−ux​x,x∈ℝ,u(t,x+1)=u(t,x),t≥0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\begin{split}&m_{t}+k_{1}\big(2\mu(u)u-u^{2}_{x})m\big)_{x}+k_{2}(2mu_{x}+um_{x})=0,\quad t>0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad m=\mu(u)-u_{xx},\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &u(t,x+1)=u(t,x),\quad t\geq 0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{split}\end{array}\right. (3.1)

In the following, for a given Banach space ZZ, we denote its norm by ∥⋅∥Z\|\cdot\|_{Z}. Various positive constants will be uniformly denoted by common letters cc or CC, which are only allowed to depend on the initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x).

The notions of strong (or classical) and weak solutions will be needed.

If u∈C⁡([0,T],Hs)∩C1​([0,T],Hs−1)u\in C([0,T];H^{s})\cap C^{1}([0,T];H^{s-1}) with s>52s>\frac{5}{2} and some T>0T>0 satisfies (3.1), then uu is called a strong solution of (1.1) on [0,T][0,T]. If u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is a strong solution on [0,T][0,T] for every T>0T>0, then it is called a global strong solution.

Lemma 3.4.

‖[Λr,f]​g‖L2≤c⁡(‖∂xf‖L∞​‖Λr−1​g‖L2+‖Λr​f‖L2​‖g‖L∞),\|[\Lambda^{r},f]g\|_{L^{2}}\leq c(\|\partial_{x}f\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Lambda^{r-1}g\|_{L^{2}}+\|\Lambda^{r}f\|_{L^{2}}\|g\|_{L^{\infty}}),

where cc is a constant depending only on rr.

The following estimates for solutions to the one-dimensional transport equation have been used in [16, 26].

Lemma 3.5.

[2, 16] Consider the one-dimensional linear transport equation

∂tf+v​∂xf=g,f|t=0=f0.\partial_{t}f+v\,\partial_{x}f=g,\quad f|_{t=0}=f_{0}. (3.11)

Let 0≤σ<10\leq\sigma<1, and suppose that

f0∈Hσ,\displaystyle f_{0}\in H^{\sigma}, g∈L1​([0,T],Hσ),\displaystyle\quad g\in L^{1}([0,T];H^{\sigma}),
vx∈L1​([0,T],L∞),\displaystyle v_{x}\in L^{1}([0,T];L^{\infty}), f∈L∞​([0,T],Hσ)∩C⁡([0,T],𝒮′).\displaystyle\quad f\in L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{\sigma})\cap C([0,T];\mathcal{S}^{\prime}).

Then f∈C⁡([0,T],Hσ)f\in C([0,T];H^{\sigma}). More precisely, there exists a constant CC depending only on σ\sigma such that, for every 0<t≤T0<t\leq T,

‖f⁡(t)‖Hσ≤eC​V​(t)​(‖f0‖Hσ+C​∫0t‖g⁡(τ)‖Hσ​dτ)withV⁡(t)=∫0t‖∂xv⁡(τ)‖L∞​dτ.\begin{split}\|f(t)\|_{H^{\sigma}}\leq&e^{CV(t)}\Big(\|f_{0}\|_{H^{\sigma}}+C\int_{0}^{t}\|g(\tau)\|_{H^{\sigma}}d\tau\Big)\quad\hbox{\it with}\quad V(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{x}v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,d\tau.\end{split}

As for the periodic case, thanks to Lemma 3.9 in [6], we know that for every u∈H1​(𝕊)u\in H^{1}({\mathbb{S}})

‖u‖μ2≤‖u‖H12≤3​‖u‖μ2\displaystyle\|u\|^{2}_{\mu}\leq\|u\|^{2}_{H^{1}}\leq 3\|u\|^{2}_{\mu}

where

∥u∥μ2=((μ−∂x2)u,u)L2=μ2(u)+∫𝕊ux2dx,\|u\|^{2}_{\mu}=\left.((\mu-\partial^{2}_{x})u,u\right.)_{L^{2}}=\mu^{2}(u)+\int_{{{S}}}u^{2}_{x}\ dx,

which implies that the norm ∥⋅∥μ\|\cdot\|_{\mu} is equivalent to the norm ∥⋅∥H1\|\cdot\|_{H^{1}}.

4. Peaked solutions

It is known that a remarkable property to the CH and μ\mu-CH equations is the existence of single and multi-peakons. In this section, we are concerned with the existence of single and multi-peakons to Eq.(1.1). Recall first that the single peakon and multi-peakons for μ\mu-CH equation and modified μ\mu-CH equation. Their single peakons are given respectively by [30]

u⁡(t,x)=1213​c​g​(x−c​t),\displaystyle u(t,x)=\frac{12}{13}cg(x-ct), (4.1)

and [42]

u⁡(t,x)=2​3​c5​g​(x−c​t),\displaystyle u(t,x)=\frac{2\sqrt{3c}}{5}g(x-ct), (4.2)

where

g⁡(x)=12​(x−[x]−12)2+2324\displaystyle g(x)=\frac{1}{2}(x-[x]-\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{23}{24}

with [x][x] denoting the largest integer part of xx. Their multi-peakons are given by

u⁡(t,x)=∑i=1Npi​(t)​g​(x−qi​(t)),\displaystyle u(t,x)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}(t)g(x-q^{i}(t)), (4.3)

where pi​(t)p_{i}(t) and qi​(t)q^{i}(t) satisfy the following ODE system respectively for the μ\mu-CH equation [32]

p˙i(t)=−∑j=1Npipjgx(qi−qj),q˙i(t)=∑j=1Npjg(qi(t)−qj(t)),i=1,2,⋯,N,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\dot{p}_{i}(t)=-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}g_{x}(q^{i}-q^{j}),\\ &\dot{q}^{i}(t)=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{N}p_{j}g(q^{i}(t)-q^{j}(t)),\;\;i=1,2,\cdots,N,\\ \end{aligned}

and for the modified μ\mu-CH equation (1.1) [42]

p˙i​(t)=0,q˙i​(t)=112​[∑j,k≠iN(pj+pk)2+25​pi2]+pi​[∑j≠iNpj​((qi−qj+12​λi​j)2+4912)]+∑j<k,j,k≠iNpjpk(qj−qk+ϵj​k)2,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \dot{p}_{i}(t)=&0,\\ \dot{q}^{i}(t)=&\frac{1}{12}\Big[\sum\limits_{j,k\not=i}^{N}(p_{j}+p_{k})^{2}+25p_{i}^{2}\Big]+p_{i}\Big[\sum\limits_{j\not=i}^{N}p_{j}\big((q^{i}-q^{j}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{ij})^{2}+\frac{49}{12}\big)\Big]\\ &+\sum\limits_{j<k,j,k\not=i}^{N}p_{j}p_{k}(q^{j}-q^{k}+\epsilon_{jk})^{2},\end{aligned}

where gxg_{x} ia defined by (3), and

λi​j={1,i<j−1,i>j,ϵj​k={1,k−j≥20,k−j≤1,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\lambda_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}1,\quad i<j\\ -1,\quad i>j,\end{array}\right.\\ &\epsilon_{jk}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}1,\quad k-j\geq 2\\ 0,\quad k-j\leq 1,\end{array}\right.\end{aligned} (4.4)

Recall that the single peakon of the CH equation (1.5) and the modified CH equation (1.7) are given respectively by [4]

u=c​e−|x−c​t|\displaystyle u=ce^{-|x-ct|}

and [27]

u=3​c2​e−|x−c​t|.\displaystyle u=\sqrt{\frac{3c}{2}}e^{-|x-ct|}.

Their periodic peakons are given respectively by [10, 43]

u=ccosh⁡(12)​cosh⁡(12−(x−c​t)+[x−c​t])\displaystyle u=\frac{c}{\cosh(\frac{1}{2})}\cosh\big(\frac{1}{2}-(x-ct)+[x-ct]\big)

and [43]

5. The local well-posedness

In this section, we shall discuss the local well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (3.1). Our result is the following theorem:

Theorem 5.1.

Suppose that u0∈Hs​(𝕊)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{S}) for some constant s>5/2s>5/2. Then there exists T>0T>0, which depends only on ‖u0‖Hs\|u_{0}\|_{H^{s}}, such that problem (3.1) has a unique solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) in the space C⁡([0,T),Hs​(𝕊))​⋂C1​([0,T),Hs−1​(𝕊))C([0,T);H^{s}(\mathbb{S}))\bigcap C^{1}([0,T);H^{s-1}(\mathbb{S})). Moreover, the solution uu depends continuously on the initial data u0u_{0} in the sense that the mapping of the initial data to the solution is continuous from the Sobolev space HsH^{s} to the space C⁡([0,T),Hs​(𝕊))​⋂C1​([0,T),Hs−1​(𝕊))C([0,T);H^{s}(\mathbb{S}))\bigcap C^{1}([0,T);H^{s-1}(\mathbb{S})).

In the remaining part of this section, we will concentrate on proving this theorem. The proof is approached by the viscosity method, which has been applied to establish the local well-posedness for the KdV equation [3] and the CH equation [33].

Firstly, we consider the Cauchy problem for a regularized version of the first equation of (3.1).

7. Wave-breaking mechanism

In this section, we give some sufficient conditions for the breaking of waves for the initial-value problem (3.1). In the case of μ0=μ⁡(u0)=0,\mu_{0}=\mu(u_{0})=0, we have the following blow-up result.

Theorem 7.1.

Let k1>0k_{1}>0, k2>0k_{2}>0 and u0∈Hsu_{0}\in H^{s}, s>5/2s>5/2, u0≠0u_{0}\neq 0 with μ0=0\mu_{0}=0. Let T>0T>0 be the maximal time of existence of the corresponding solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) of (3.1) with the initial value u0.u_{0}. Then the solution uu blows up in finite time T∗<∞.T^{*}<\infty.

Proof.

Notice that u∈C⁡([0,T),Hs)u\in C([0,T);H^{s}) is a periodic function of xx. Then there exists a x0∈𝕊x_{0}\in{{S}} such that u0,x​(x0)<0u_{0,x}(x_{0})<0. Consider the flow (6.18) with μ0=0\mu_{0}=0, i.e., the flow q⁡(t,x)q(t,x) governed by −k1​ux2+k2​u,-k_{1}u_{x}^{2}+k_{2}u,

d​qd​t=(−k1​ux2+k2​u)​(t,q⁡(t,x)),q|t=0=x.\displaystyle\frac{dq}{dt}=(-k_{1}u_{x}^{2}+k_{2}u)(t,q(t,x)),\;\;q|_{t=0}=x. (7.3)

Along with the flow q⁡(t,x)q(t,x), we deduce from (7.2) that

d​ux​(t,q⁡(t,x))d​t=ux​t+(−k1​ux2+k2​u)​ux​x=−k22​(ux2+μ12).\displaystyle\frac{du_{x}(t,q(t,x))}{dt}=u_{xt}+(-k_{1}u_{x}^{2}+k_{2}u)u_{xx}=-{\textstyle\frac{k_{2}}{2}}(u_{x}^{2}+\mu_{1}^{2}).

Let w⁡(t)=k2​ux​(t,q⁡(t,x0))w(t)=k_{2}u_{x}(t,q(t,x_{0})). It follows from the above equation that
